newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan smelters see slower profit growth this year.
newsitem.headline: Japan smelters see slower profit growth this year.

text.p: Japanese smelters said on Monday they expected a slowdown in profit growth this year after strong gains in fiscal 1996/97, when the dollar's surge against the yen dramatically boosted their earnings.
Mitsubishi Materials Corp raised some eyebrows and a bit of scepticism, however, as the only one predicting better profit growth this year than last.
Announcing their 1996/97 results, six leading non-ferrous metal refining companies issued forecasts for 1997/98 parent current profit growth ranging from 14.6 percent to 31.3 percent.
This compared with impressive growth rates of 26.9 percent to 114.9 percent at the six companies in the year ended on March 31, modestly exceeding their own and analysts' predictions.
"The figures for the past year and for the current year are pretty good. The market should welcome the results," said Minoru Hasegawa, analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

Analysts agreed higher copper output, a recovery in zinc business and a rebound in the electronics materials sector would boost smelters' profits, although they were unlikely to benefit from a rise in the dollar against the yen this year.
They were puzzled, however, by bullish forecasts at Mitsubishi Materials, which predicted profit growth would accelerate this year to 28.2 percent from 26.9 percent last year.
"Mitsubishi Materials' strong forecast was a surprise. I have to study their figures very carefully," Hasegawa said.

Mitsubishi Materials said: "We expect higher sales of advanced and silicon products mainly for information technology equipment. At the same time, we should benefit from divisional rationalisations and lower indirect costs."

Analysts' scepticism reflected views that Mitsubishi Materials was struggling in the beverage can business, as well as in the concrete and silicon sectors. They also noted its profits were small in relation to sales.

"Earnings in the silicon business will be flat at best, while they are likely to see lower profits in cement and aluminium cans," said Jiro Iokibe, analyst at Daiwa Institute of Research. "I'm not sure if they can achieve what they say."
Against the recent backdrop of strong international metal prices, many smelters have already announced that their copper and zinc refineries are running at full capacity.
Analysts said that, while 1997 treatment charges for copper were raised only marginally, strong zinc prices would more than offset a cut in zinc treatment charges.
Koichi Hariya, analyst at Nikko Research Center, said companies that can capitalise most on a recovery since last autumn in the electronics materials sector would fare best.
Analysts' favorite remained Mitsui Mining and Smelting Co Ltd, which they said was in the strongest position in the copper foil sector.
"I'd recommend Mitsui. They have highly competitive electronics materials such as copper foil and materials for liquid crystal displays," said Daiwa's Iokibe.

The six firms forecast the following parent current profits for the fiscal 1997/98 year, which ends on March 31, 1998 (in billions of yen unless specified; year-on-year percentage change in brackets):
Mitsubishi Materials Corp 13.50(+28.2) 10.53(+26.9)
Sumitomo Metal Mining 14.50(+15.4) 12.56(+39.1)
Mitsui Mining and Smelting 10.50(+15.8) 9.07(+78.4)
Dowa Mining Co Ltd 8.00(+18.0) 6.78(+78.4)
-- Tokyo Commodities Desk +81-3-3432-7431
